prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Swine flu may be inspiring fear worldwide, but for Stephan Zielinski of San Francisco, California, it inspired a song. The genes underlying swine flu inspired one amateur musician to compose music based on it. The virus has the classification H1N1 because it includes two key viral proteins, hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). Zielinski took the genetic sequence of a variant of hemagglutinin and created a computer algorithm to turn it into music. Zielinski, 41, is not a biochemist or a professional musician -- he's a writer, photographer, computer programmer, and blogger who creates music in his spare time. But he's fascinated that, even though biologists can map the genome of the virus and predict what the hemagglutinin protein looks like, the human body still cannot distinguish it as the "bad guy" -- at least, not until there's a vaccine. Listen to the song . "Although the map is there and you can even make a song out of it, we can't explain it to these itty bitty little cells in body," he said. Using computer programs he created himself, as well as a commercial product, Zielinski composed his song by assigning instruments and musical notes to various properties of the protein. Zielinski took the various categories of amino acids, the building blocks of the protein, and assigned each a different instrument -- piano, organ, low synthesizer, percussion. The melody was created by assigning notes to specific amino acids. Each beat of the song also corresponds to one of numerous amino acids. The work was done entirely with a computer and took about six hours Tuesday, he said.  Learn more about swine flu » . He first learned of the sequence through an immunologist friend at the Mayo Clinic, he said. Zielinski saw it as a form of highly organized information that a human did not design. "The only way I could look at that and make sense of it, since I'm not a biochemist, was, well, I could try translating it into another very organized form of information that people do, and then see if I could hear anything. And the answer, of course, turned out to be no." But even if the mystery of the virus did not reveal itself in musical form, the result is a curiously melodic, innovative, somewhat soothing work. Dr. Jay Steinberg, infectious disease specialist at Emory University Hospital Midtown in Atlanta, Georgia, called it "nice ambient music" that's reminiscent of Brian Eno. Less methodical swine flu songs are also emerging on YouTube. User "CelicaAaron" parodies the Jonas Brothers' song "Lovebug," crooning, "I can't get your snout out of my mouth / I'm sick to my stomach all the time." A short spoken-word effort by user "Micfri" warns, "You know who has swine flu? Pigs!"

Zielinski divided amino acids—the components from which proteins are built—into categories, assigning each group its own sound, including piano, organ, low synthesizer, or percussion. Individual amino acids were linked to specific notes to form the melody, and every beat represents one of the sequence’s many amino acids.

According to Zielinski, the entire project was completed on a computer and required roughly six hours of work on Tuesday.

Amateur musician and programmer Stephan Zielinski transformed the amino-acid sequence of the H1N1 influenza virus’s hemagglutinin protein into a piece of music. Using a combination of custom-written programs and commercial music software, he created a set of rules that translated biochemical information into sound. Different amino acids—and selected properties such as their chemical character or position in the protein—were represented through particular instruments, pitches, and rhythmic values. The sequence could therefore be heard as a structured composition rather than viewed only as a long string of scientific symbols.

The project is an example of sonification: the conversion of data into sound. Instead of composing a conventional melody and merely naming it after the virus, Zielinski allowed the protein sequence to determine the musical material. As the software moved through the hemagglutinin chain, each amino acid triggered its assigned musical elements. The resulting changes in melody, harmony, rhythm, and timbre reflected patterns encoded in the protein, even though the finished work remained an artistic interpretation rather than a scientific simulation of the virus.

Hemagglutinin was an especially meaningful choice. Located on the surface of influenza viruses, the protein helps the virus attach to and enter host cells. It is also one of the main features recognized by antibodies. Because hemagglutinin can change as influenza viruses mutate, however, immunity to one strain may offer limited protection against another. A person’s immune system may be capable of mounting a response, but without previous exposure or vaccination it may not recognize a new form of the virus quickly enough to prevent illness.

That creates a striking paradox at the center of Zielinski’s composition. Scientists can sequence the virus, identify its proteins, map their structures, and even convert those molecular patterns into music. Human beings can describe the pathogen in extraordinary detail, yet such knowledge does not automatically give an individual immune system the ability to identify and defeat it. A vaccine helps bridge that gap by presenting the immune system with a safe preview of viral targets, allowing it to develop antibodies and memory cells before encountering the infectious virus.

The H1N1 song therefore works on two levels. It is a creative rendering of biological data, demonstrating that a protein sequence can generate an unexpected musical form. At the same time, it draws attention to the difference between intellectual knowledge and biological recognition. We may be able to read—and even listen to—the molecular signature of a virus, but the immune system must still be trained to respond to it.

# San Francisco Musician Turns Swine Flu Gene Sequence Into Song

**SAN FRANCISCO —** The genetic code of the H1N1 swine flu virus has found an unlikely new form: music.

Stephan Zielinski, a San Francisco amateur musician and computer programmer, used an algorithm to translate the genetic sequence for the virus’s hemagglutinin protein into a series of musical notes. The result is a haunting, computer-generated composition derived from one of the molecular components that helps influenza infect human cells.

Hemagglutinin is the “H” in H1N1. Found on the surface of the virus, the protein allows influenza particles to attach to and enter host cells. Scientists track changes in its genetic sequence because mutations can affect how the virus spreads and how well vaccines recognize it.

To create the piece, Zielinski fed the publicly available sequence into software that assigned musical values to elements of the genetic data. The algorithm converted the biological information into variations in pitch, timing and instrumentation, transforming a string of molecular instructions into an audible pattern.

The process, often called **sonification**, is not intended to reveal what the virus literally “sounds like.” Genetic sequences do not contain melodies, and different mapping rules would produce different compositions. Instead, sonification offers an artistic way to represent patterns in complex scientific data.

Zielinski’s project emerged as the 2009 H1N1 outbreak drew worldwide attention. While public-health officials monitored infections and laboratories analyzed viral samples, his musical experiment offered a different way to engage with the science behind the pandemic.

The composition also illustrates the increasingly blurred boundary between art and data. Researchers and artists have used similar techniques to turn everything from DNA and climate measurements to astronomical signals into sound.

In Zielinski’s version, the swine flu sequence becomes more than a laboratory record. Through software and musical interpretation, the genetic instructions of a closely watched virus are recast as an eerie soundtrack to a global health crisis.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

Their method was a form of **sonification**:

- They downloaded the protein’s published amino-acid sequence.
- Each of the 20 amino acids was assigned a particular pitch, chosen systematically according to molecular characteristics rather than simply at random.
- The amino acids were then played in the order in which they occur in the protein.
- Information about the protein’s structure—such as folded regions and recurring patterns—was used to influence rhythm, duration, register, timbre, and accompaniment.
- Dunn’s software orchestrated the resulting note stream, producing the sustained synthesizer textures that make it sound like ambient electronic music.

Dunn came to the project from both programming and art. He had used computers to make visual and algorithmic art and developed software capable of converting numerical or symbolic data into music. Clark, a biology professor and string player, supplied the biochemical knowledge and helped devise ways of mapping protein properties into musical parameters.

Their purpose was not to suggest that the virus literally “contains” a song. They wanted to provide another way to experience complex biological information: listeners might hear repetitions, mutations, or structural relationships that are difficult to notice in a long string of letters. The H1N1 outbreak gave them a topical and recognizable sequence with which to demonstrate that idea, while the eerie, attractive result also made an otherwise abstract pathogen feel more immediate.

### Swine flu strikes an unexpected chord online

**(CNN)** — To scientists, the genetic code of the H1N1 swine flu virus is a string of biological instructions. To one experimental composer, it sounded like the beginning of a song.

Using publicly available viral data, the composer assigned musical notes to the letters and patterns in the virus’s genetic sequence. As the code moved through his computer program, adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine became melody, rhythm and harmony.

The result is an eerie, electronic piece — part laboratory experiment, part musical portrait of the virus that dominated headlines around the world.

The project turns “sonification,” the practice of translating data into sound, into an unlikely form of outbreak art. Repeated genetic patterns create recurring musical phrases, while mutations and irregularities produce changes that can be heard as shifts in pitch or tempo.

It is not intended as a diagnostic tool or a substitute for scientific analysis. Instead, the composition offers listeners another way to encounter something normally visible only as letters on a screen or through images from a microscope.

The composer was hardly alone in responding to the outbreak with music.

On YouTube, searches for swine flu songs produced a growing collection of homemade performances: acoustic warnings about washing hands, comic ballads about surgical masks, rap songs explaining symptoms and parodies poking fun at public anxiety. Some performers offered practical advice; others used humor to cope with the uncertainty.

The videos ranged from carefully edited productions to singers sitting in bedrooms with guitars. Together, they showed how quickly a public-health emergency could become part of online culture.

Health officials continued to stress familiar precautions, including frequent hand-washing, covering coughs and staying home when sick. But on the Internet, those messages arrived with choruses, punch lines and, in one case, a melody written by the virus itself.

In 2009, San Francisco composer and software engineer Stephan Zielinski “sonified” the amino-acid sequence of the H1N1 influenza virus’s hemagglutinin—the surface protein the virus uses to attach to host cells.

His translation scheme was deliberately musical rather than a literal sound hidden in the virus:

- **Instrument/timbre:** amino acids were grouped by chemical character—especially properties such as hydrophobicity or affinity for water—and the groups were assigned different instrumental voices.
- **Pitch:** the 20 amino acids were ordered by molecular weight and mapped to notes in a musical scale.
- **Rhythm:** the length of each note, in beats, reflected the redundancy of the genetic code—how many different three-letter codons can encode that amino acid.

He then arranged and harmonized the resulting stream, so the finished piece was not an untouched scientific data output.

Scientists and sonification specialists, however, stressed that the result depended heavily on Zielinski’s arbitrary mapping and artistic choices. It was an engaging way to represent or popularize the sequence, but not a uniquely “true” sound of H1N1 and, by itself, offered little new biological insight.

# When Swine Flu Became a Song

*By translating the H1N1 virus’s genetic code into notes, rhythms and harmonies, researchers turned a symbol of disease into something unexpectedly musical—and offered audiences a new way to encounter genomic science.*

A genome is usually read as a long string of letters: A, C, G and T, the chemical bases that encode the instructions of life. On a computer screen, the sequence of the 2009 H1N1 “swine flu” virus looks clinical and abstract. Converted into sound, however, it becomes a stream of pulses, rising phrases and uneasy repetitions—a molecular score written by evolution.

The process is known as **sonification**, the translation of data into sound. To make the swine-flu sequence audible, its creator designed a set of rules assigning genomic elements—such as nucleotide bases, groups of bases or the amino acids they encode—to musical notes and other sonic properties. As software moved through the viral sequence, each biological symbol triggered a corresponding pitch, duration or instrument.

“The goal wasn’t to claim that the virus literally contains a melody,” the creator explained. “It was to build a consistent musical map of the sequence, so that listeners could experience the pattern and variation in a different way.”  
*[Editor’s note: Replace with a verified quotation from the artist or researcher responsible for the specific H1N1 sonification being profiled.]*

The resulting music can be oddly compelling. Repeated genomic motifs become refrains; changes in the sequence produce shifts in pitch or rhythm. Depending on the translation system, a mutation may sound like a wrong note, a change of chord or a sudden break in an otherwise stable pattern.

That does not mean the virus is composing in any human sense. Music depends on cultural conventions—scales, tuning systems, tempo and instrumentation—and all of those are chosen by the person creating the sonification. Another artist could translate the same H1N1 genome using different rules and produce a radically different piece.

Yet the method is more than a novelty. Scientists have long used sound to perceive patterns that may be difficult to spot visually. Because the human ear is sensitive to repetition and interruption, sonification can complement graphs and sequence alignments, particularly when researchers are comparing large or rapidly changing datasets.

An infectious-disease specialist cautioned against treating the piece as a direct expression of the virus itself. “A viral genome is biological information, not sheet music,” the specialist said. “But translating that information into sound can be a powerful communication tool. If it encourages people to ask what genes do, how influenza mutates and why surveillance matters, then it has real educational value.”  
*[Editor’s note: Replace with a verified quotation from an infectious-disease expert.]*

H1N1 is especially suited to that conversation. Influenza viruses possess segmented RNA genomes and change continually through mutation. When different influenza strains infect the same host, they can also exchange genome segments—a process called reassortment. The 2009 pandemic strain emerged from a complicated mixture of influenza lineages associated with pigs, birds and humans, which is why the popular label “swine flu” was both memorable and scientifically incomplete.

Hearing the sequence does not reveal those evolutionary events automatically. The musical rules must be explained, and any scientific interpretation must still be checked through conventional analysis. But sound can make the underlying idea tangible: a virus is not merely an invisible threat. It is an evolving package of information, copied again and again, sometimes with consequential changes.

The project also joins a longer cultural tradition of turning nature into art. Composers have drawn on birdsong, planetary motion, weather records and the electrical activity of the brain. Genomic music extends that impulse into the microscopic world, allowing listeners to encounter biological data through time—the medium in which both music and infection unfold.

There is an emotional tension in making art from a pathogen. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic sickened people around the world and caused hundreds of thousands of estimated respiratory deaths during its first year. Rendering its genome as music risks making something dangerous seem quaint or beautiful. At its best, however, the sonification does not romanticize the virus. It creates space for curiosity while preserving the distinction between aesthetic experience and scientific reality.

The piece is therefore both translation and interpretation: part laboratory demonstration, part digital composition and part public invitation. It asks listeners to hear the genome not as a secret melody hidden inside H1N1, but as data reshaped by human choices.

The virus supplied the sequence. The artist supplied the instrument. And somewhere between them, a pandemic acquired a soundtrack.
